<PubmedArticle><MedlineCitation Status="MEDLINE" Owner="NLM" IndexingMethod="Manual"><PMID Version="1">7878473</PMID><DateCompleted><Year>1995</Year><Month>04</Month><Day>06</Day></DateCompleted><DateRevised><Year>2025</Year><Month>01</Month><Day>22</Day></DateRevised><Article PubModel="Print"><Journal><ISSN IssnType="Print">0036-8075</ISSN><JournalIssue CitedMedium="Print"><Volume>267</Volume><Issue>5203</Issue><PubDate><Year>1995</Year><Month>Mar</Month><Day>10</Day></PubDate></JournalIssue><Title>Science (New York, N.Y.)</Title><ISOAbbreviation>Science</ISOAbbreviation></Journal><ArticleTitle>Storage of 7 +/- 2 short-term memories in oscillatory subcycles.</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>1512</StartPage><EndPage>1515</EndPage><MedlinePgn>1512-5</MedlinePgn></Pagination><Abstract><AbstractText>Psychophysical measurements indicate that human subjects can store approximately seven short-term memories. Physiological studies suggest that short-term memories are stored by patterns of neuronal activity. Here it is shown that activity patterns associated with multiple memories can be stored in a single neural network that exhibits nested oscillations similar to those recorded from the brain. Each memory is stored in a different high-frequency ("40 hertz") subcycle of a low-frequency oscillation. Memory patterns repeat on each low-frequency (5 to 12 hertz) oscillation, a repetition that relies on activity-dependent changes in membrane excitability rather than reverberatory circuits. This work suggests that brain oscillations are a timing mechanism for controlling the serial processing of short-term memories.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author
